fr:title.text: Precursor to The Core of Adjoint Functors

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Precursor to The Core of Adjoint Functors

fr:mainmatter.fr:p: Mentioned in passing as 2.1. Proposition., as "well-known".

fr:ul.fr:li: Suppose U : A → X is a functor, F : X .ob → A .ob a function, and (πₓ : A(F(x), -) ≅ X(x, U(-)))_{x ∈ X} a family of natural isomorphisms. Then there is a unique extension \overline {F} of F such that (πₓ)_{x ∈ X} is natural in x, witnessing \overline {F} ⊣ U.
Or dually, suppose that F is a functor, but U is just a function on objects, and (πₐ : A(F(-), a) ≅ X(-, U(a)))_{a ∈ A}. Then U uniquely extends to \overline {U}.

fr:mainmatter.fr:p: Let's be pedantic and clarify that A(F(-), -), X(-, U(-)): Xᵒᵖ → Setᴬ have the same action on morphisms as Hom(-, -)∘Fᵒᵖ, λx. Hom(x, -)∘U. This is conventionally left implicit, but we remark to clarify what we mean by the family of natural isomorphisms being natural.
NOTE: I couldn't get よ to render in the latex (diagrams). I'm not sure if it's a lualatex/dvi or font issue.

We take inspiration from the thin case. We wts the F-action on morphisms is fully determined already (∃!). That is, we have two goals:
(∃) Show that there is a suitable F-action.
(!) That any other F-action is equal to it. As usual, let η_x = πₓ(F(x))(1_{F(x)}) : X(x, U∘F(x)) denote the component of the unit of the (a posteriori) adjunction and ϵₐ = π_{U(a)}(a)⁻¹(1_{U(a)}) denote the component of the counit.

fr:ul.fr:li:
(!)
To finish off the result, we wts for any other F' extending F to morphisms st F' ⊣ U, witnessed by π : Xᵒᵖ → Setᴬ, that F' = \overline {F}. This simply follows from the observation that ∀f. naturality of π is exactly this square, and forces よ(F'(f)) = πₓ⁻¹∘(-∘f)∘π_y = よ(\overline {F}(f))

fr:mainmatter.fr:p: So this result is really a corollary of the Yoneda lemma. The nlab page is here.

Of course in hindsight, we could've (or even should've) just defined \overline {F} to be よ⁻¹(πₓ⁻¹∘(-∘f)∘π_y) from the get-go, since it's a much more clearly well-behaved definition, but unless you're already sold on the Yoneda principle, I find it a difficult leap without struggling with lower-level objects a bit first. I'm still in training.
This is the perspective taken in the short proof.
However, unlike the thin case, we crucially use the information that U is a functor so the natural transformation squares are well-defined.
The first point:

During my Topology lectures at Macquarie University in the 1970s, the students and I realized, in proving that a function f between posets was order preserving when there was a function u in the reverse direction such that f (x) ≤ a if and only if x ≤ u(a), did not require u to be order preserving. I realized then that knowing functors in the two directions only on objects and the usual hom adjointness isomorphism implied the effect of the functors on homs was uniquely determined. Writing this down properly led to the present paper.

fr:title.text: The core of adjoint monotone functions

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The core of adjoint monotone functions

fr:mainmatter.fr:p: This is mentioned in passing, in the intro to The Core of Adjoint Functors.
Suppose P and Q are posets, f : P → Q is a priori just a function, and u : P ← Q monotone, such that f(x) ≤ a ⟺ x ≤ u(a). Then f monotone as well.
Or dually, suppose that f monotone, but u is a priori just a function. Then u monotone as well.
Suppose p₁ ≤ p₂. Notice that p₂ ≤ u∘f(p₂), by the unit of the (thin) adjunction. Then p₁ ≤ p₂ ≤ u∘f(p₂) ⟹ f(p₁) ≤ f(p₂) by the Hom bijection of the (thin) adjunction.
(dual) Suppose q₁ ≤ q₂. Notice that f∘u(q₁) ≤ q₂ by the counit of the (thin) adjunction. Then f∘u(q₁) ≤ q₁ ≤ q₂ ⟹ u(q₁) ≤ u(q₂) by the Hom bijection of the (thin) adjunction.

Notice that the above proof does not use the information that u is monotone. Thus the above lemma holds where f and u are just a priori functions. The above lemma is in some sense the more immediately natural question, but can be easily strengthened to the form of this corollary.

fr:ul.fr:li: functions U : A .ob → X .ob and F : X .ob → A .ob
a family of isomorphisms (π_{x,a} : A(F(x), a) ≅ X(X, U(a)))_{a ∈ A, x ∈ X}

fr:mainmatter.fr:p: An adjunction core extends to an adjuction iff ∀a,b ∈ A. ∀x ∈ X. I commutes, and iff ∀x,y ∈ X. a ∈ A. II commutes. The adjunction is unique when it exists.
The original theorem is stated in terms of \mathcal {V}-enriched categories, but we only treat the simple case of Homset-categories here.

fr:mainmatter.fr:p: We use the same notation and definitions of η, ϵ, \overline {F}, \overline {U} as the explicit proof of the precursor lemma. The definition of \overline {F}, \overline {U} in the short proof presupposes that U is a functor, so we're scrupulous to avoid circularity.
This proof is rather low tech and is lifted straight from the paper. It's also how you'd attack the precursor head-on. The utility is that it holds in enriched categories.

The forward directions are trivial. Suppose (F, U, (π_{a, x})_{a ∈ A, x ∈ X}) extends to \overline {F} ⊣_π \overline {U}. Then I expresses that ∀g : A(a, b). ∀f : A(F(x), a). π_{x, b}(g∘f) = \overline {U}(g)∘π_{a, x}(f). This is exactly the condition that ∀g : A(a, b). π is natural in a at g, which is certainly true of an adjunction. II expresses something similar (dual).
The nontrivial directions are the backward directions.

fr:li.fr:p: (I) wts I ⟹ \overline {U} is a functor. Suppose ∀a,b ∈ A. ∀x ∈ X. I holds. Then in particular, ∀c ∈ A. I holds at x = U(c).

fr:li.fr:p: Combined with the earlier proof that \overline {U}(1ₐ) = 1_{\overline {U}(a)} (which just follows by definition), we've shown that \overline {U} defines a functorial action on morphisms. Actually, we saw earlier that I expresses that π is natural in a, so we've met the preconditions of the precursor lemma, thus there is a unique extension \overline {F} st \overline {F} ⊣_π \overline {U}.
There's two ways ways to see the uniqueness situation:

fr:ul.fr:li: (Going backwards) Since the definitions of \overline {F} and \overline {U} (in the precursor) are not dependent on the other functor, the total adjunction \overline {F} ⊣ \overline {U} is the unique one extending the core by applying the uniqueness result of the precusor to each functor in turn, just knowing the other is a well-defined functor.

fr:li.fr:p: (II) wts II ⟹ \overline {F} is a functor. This is dual.

fr:mainmatter.fr:p: (For V-enriched categories, ) If V is thin, all diagrams commute, thus an adjunction core always determines an adjunction.
Set isn't thin, but 2 is, thus for posets, an adjunction core gives rise to a thin adjunction, as remarked here. I don't know how useful this lemma is for ordinary Homset categories.
